COVID-19 Border Post Chaos: A Day in The Life of A Crosser

By: Busisiwe Gumede | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
From bribing officials to crossing the crocodile infested Limpopo River by foot, these Zimbabwean border jumpers are risking it all for a better life in SA.

Unique Selling Point:
Images of panic and overcrowding at the Beitbridge border post are familiar enough to anyone who was watching the nightly television news over the festive season. But the reality and pain of such a life is unimaginable for most of us.
In this report, we take a closer look at a day in the life of an illegal Zimbabwean border jumper. We take an emotional journey that uncovers who they are, the dangerous and illegal routes they use to cross into SA and how that is expected to affect our country's efforts of fighting COVID-19.

Summary:
According to reports, thousands of desperate Zimbabwean nationals who were trying to cross into South Africa are no longer camping at the Beitbridge border post. But that doesn’t mean that they have returned to their Zimbabwean homes. Some have resorted to illegal and clandestine ways, like riding on canoes or bribing soldiers, to worm their way back into South Africa via the Limpopo River. This investigation explores how such longstanding issues of border security stand to hamper South Africa's fight against COVID-19.


Further information:
In this report, we will speak to two case studies BEFORE their desperate attempt to cross via one of the 18 ports of entry of the Limpopo river. These people will share with us who they are, why they want to cross, their fears and hopes and aspirations for a better life in South Africa.

In addition, we speak to one of the illegal operators of canoes, which are mostly used to carry people over to the SA side. These men accept money from travellers and their job is to transport them into SOuth Africa. How difficult is this job? Why aren't they getting caught? They will tell you that a big reason why they aren't in jail is because of the relationship that they have with the authorities, which, according to them, they share their profits with.

We also attempt to answer questions around how such operations affect our COVID-19 infection numbers. Illegal crossers obviously don't require a negative COVID-19 test result to come into South Africa. How much of this is a threat to our health?

Extra Budget Items:
Case studies can only be found and filmed at the boarder BEFORE making their cross to SA. For this, a Zimbabwean fixer/journalist has been identified to do the job. Travel, accommodation and filming fee fixed at R6000.

In addition, transport fees to Musina will be required for the producer, presenter and cameraman. Here is a proposed breakdown:

For two cars - Presenter and Producer + Camera man

Shoot day to Musina will be in and out, as such no accommodation costs will apply. So petrol and tollgate money is as follows:

1. R1 200 for tolls ( about R600 each car to and back). To save on this, a big car could be used instead to accommodate the crew.

2. R3 000 (R1500 full tank x 2).


Expert:
Ms. Liesl Louw-Vaudran

Locations:
Zimbabwe
Gauteng and also Musina( Limpopo)

Other Footage Sources:
Twitter videos that trended four weeks ago.

Hidden Camera: Yes
Reason for hidden camera: Hidden camera to be used to expose the illegal activity happening at the border. There are reports of officials including members of the army taking bribes to keep quiet about illegal jumpers. This may be exposed as part of our investigation.

Legal: Yes
Reason for legal: The assistance of leal may be required depending on the kind of footage that we will find. Since we will be exposing illegal activity that is happening in another country and at some points doing so via spy camera footage, we need to protect ourselves.

Graphics: Yes
Reason for graphics: Illustration of the various points of the Limpopo River and also putting into perspective how long the border fence is through map graphics.

Press Release:


Running the Gauntlet – How Border Crossers reach SA or The Influx of Illegal Migrants

As the Beitbridge Border Post re-opens after more than a month of lockdown that sought to stop the spread of COVID-19 Minister of Home Affairs Dr Aaron Motsoaledi has said people arriving at the border with forged COVID-19 test results would be refused access and barred from South Africa for at least five years. But that has not stopped migrants, desperate to get back to jobs and families in this country from risking life and limb to cross the border. Carte Blanche investigates the risks and costs of getting across the treacherous terrain.

Script:


VO: On Monday this past week, the Beitbridge Border Post was opened after being closed early in January, as a measure to stop the spread of Coronavirus.

This meant that Zimbabwean nationals who had gone home for the festive season wouldn't be able to cross back into South Africa without presenting a work permit and a valid COVID-19 test certificate.

These are documents that this 39 year old man, doesn’t have. We call him Thabane. Apart from not having R1000 for a COVID-19 test, he simply doesn’t have a passport.

His best chance of being reunited with his wife in Johannesburg is by paying a black-market guide. He meets up with his guide after a 15KM journey on foot, from his home village of Gwanda.

Thabane agreed to speak to us where the guide dropped him off, a few meters on the South African side of the border.

THABANE: 14:02 For me to get here I had to navigate dangerous places and risk my life so I can take care of my children. because the border is closed.

THABANE: 01:12 We found some man who could help us and we paid him R400 and he went to speak to the police.

VO: Thabane has been living and working as a plumber in South Africa since 2002. But the anxiety of long-distance parenting compelled him to visit his frail parents who are raising his two children.

11:57 Yes, my parents raised me but in a different era. I would love to raise my own children but it’s hard because I can't live with them because of the situation in Zimbabwe.
02:14 The situation in Zimbabwe is bad, you cannot live there. There is no work.

VO: In order to give his family a better quality of life, Thabane had to leave Zimbabwe.

THABANE: 04:53 Things are expensive in Zimbabwe. We only send money when school fees are due.

((MAC: Link 1 - With extra covid-prevention measures heightened...

How are illegal immigrants still able to cross into SA without COVID-19 screening & certification?

VO: Thabane intended to cross the Limpopo River by canoe…recent rains mean the river is in full flood.

Amateur footage taken on the Zimbabwean side of the Limpopo shows the challenges for migrants. The river is unforgiving and several men and women play a waiting game before trusting instructors to help and guide them across.
The man in the grey shirt, Farai says it’s all about the skill of the instructors.

Crosser on Zim side: 00:48 We have boys who have learnt how the water flows. They have expertise in facilitating us to cross to where we want to go. Yes we agree the river is full but now you might die of Corona or hunger. If the river takes me that means I was going to die anyways.

VO: On water, a simple mistake, like not listening can cost you your life.

01:59 These boys here they do their jb proper and we just try to follow and respect their line of work. We sneak our way through the river and avoid getting caught by officials.

VO: For some river guides, the job is an act of mercy and they’re also supplying a demand. A service that David Chimbili charges less than R100 for.

01:10 From here to the river they pay R50 on those little boats and then they go to Musina, that’s where they will get transport to go further and others stay to buy in Musina.

VO: Although it may be a lot cheaper for Farai to cross on foot, surviving the flooded river can mean taking a small boat. But even that won’t guarantee his safety.

NAT SOUND OF THE VIDEO

VO: But it’s hunger that propels people to brave the Limpopo …traverse thick bushes for over 15 kilometers and jump off bridges…and amateur videos taken on the route show not a single face mask in sight.

THABANE: 16:53 This place is dangerous because sometimes when you’re walking there is water underneath and any mistake you might slip and die in the water. Even if there is no water below, you risk slipping and falling to your death.

VO: Despite not having a COVID test or a passport, many say that before the pandemic, moving between Zimbabwe and South Africa was a lot simpler. Home Affairs Minister Aaron Motswoaledi says the department is aware of the illegal activities at the border.

MAC: We are still finding that there are huge movements of people crossing from Zimbabwe to South Africa….

Minister: Its one of the issues home affairs is dealing with

VO: WHEN migrants are found to have illegally entered South Africa, they are detained at Lindela Repatriation Centre.

Head of research at Institute for Security Studies, Ottalia Maunganidze, says Lindela is a temporary solution to a permanent problem.

OTTALIA: 21:12 Repatriation centers have proven globally to be ineffective mechanisms to deter people from coming back…

VO: Applying for a Zimbabwean passport can set citizens back about R6000. And even if they do have the money, Thabane says they have to wait more than 12 months before being able to collect it. These are the reasons many choose the illegal route, says Ottilia.

Right now if you ask the department of home affairs how many people are in south africa illegally they cannot give you a right number because they do not know they will give you an estimation of between 500 000 people and four million.

VO: Thabane, who has in effect become a repeat offender is a classic example of migrants dodging the law

THABANI: 21:28 I was in quarantine before and then I was fined.
21:43 I was fined because they found I was arrested more than three times. So they were reprimanding me for repeating the same offence.

VO: This 40KM fence was erected in a project spearheaded by the Department of Public Works in a bid to manage the spread of COVID-19. This month parliament’s standing committee ON public accounts said it was hastily built and a national embarrassment.

UP SOUND OF SCOPA BITE

VO: SCOPA says no more money should be allocated to maintaining the fence which is only a year old. We reached out to the South African National Defence Force and Department of Public Works – but had no response.

Link 2

Since the Limpopo river is currently in flood, a migrant's best option could be to be smuggled by transporters who are widely known here as Malayisha.

VO: This Malayisha says he has been in the people-smuggling business for over 15 years.

MALAYISHA: 01:45 I couldn’t find a job in Zimbabwe, I started doing this and got more clients.

VO: He says each situation is unique.

MALAYISHA: 05:39 Sometimes we walk through the border or at times we are on a truck. We fetch people from the Zimbabwean side at a petrol station and leave you on the South African side.

VO: He negotiates with officials from either side and pays them a fee to turn a blind eye.

To reach his final destination in Johannesburg, Thabane spent about R1000.
R400 - for the Malayisha , who smuggled him to Musina.
And R600 - to travel from the border town to Joburg.

MALAYISHA: 04:44 We have an entrance gate where you pay R100 and the exit gate, you pay R100 and the bridge there are Zimbabwean soldiers, you pay R100. On the South African side, there are police, you pay R100.

VO: Sometimes the business can be lucrative, he says.

MALAYISHA:12:17 The biggest amount I have made is on many different occasions, the bigger the load the more I made. You can have 10 border jumpers and make R6000, the more the border jumper the more you can negotiate.

He acknowledges that he is breaking the law but says the need to put food on the table far outweighs his conscience.

MALAYISHA: 00:15 We are helping people at the same time, we get money. It is better than trying to find a job and I prefer to be self-employed I think i make more money.

VO: He also prides himself on having escaped the consequences thus far.

MALAYISHA: 07:39 I have never been into a police cell since I started doing my cross-border business, I always make sure I create good relations

LINK 3 - But this is also about corrupt officials - not only on the Zimbabwean side but on the South African side too.

This Malayisha says, some people bribe themselves out of providing COVID-19 certificates.

MALAYISHA: 01:15 Here at the border, they are testing and ask for the certificate, but the issue is that if you do not have the certificate, they take money and let you go. Even if you have a certificate, they tell you it is fake and demand a bribe.

ARRON MOTSOALEDI: 10:27 we have charged a number of home affairs officials who do the types of things you are saying. That is why we want to strengthen the anti-corruption unit, but more than anything else, you are aware that in the border management act, we want to have a commissioner of borders.

VO: But it seems a better solution could be coming. The border management act was implemented last year.

11:24 The border management will coordinate that and will be able to identify syndicates because we know they exist. part of what they will do is devise play to catch these syndicates.

VO: Thabani says his intention is not to break the law …all he wants is a chance at a better life.

THABANI: 23:11I am hoping to go to SA safely and get work. Maybe the vaccines will help so things can go back to normal.

VO: Thabane, who has in effect become a repeat offender is a classic example of migrants dodging the law THABANI: 21:28 I was in quarantine before and then I was fined. 21:43 I was fined because they found I was arrested more than three times. So they were reprimanding me for repeating the same offence. VO: This 40KM fence was erected in a project spearheaded by the Department of Public Works in a bid to manage the spread of COVID-19. This month parliament’s standing committee ON public accounts said it was hastily built and a national embarrassment. UP SOUND OF SCOPA BITE VO: SCOPA says no more money should be allocated to maintaining the fence which is only a year old. We reached out to the South African National Defence Force and Department of Public Works – but had no response. Link 2 Since the Limpopo river is currently in flood, a migrant's best option could be to be smuggled by transporters who are widely known here as Malayisha. VO: This Malayisha says he has been in the people-smuggling business for over 15 years. MALAYISHA: 01:45 I couldn’t find a job in Zimbabwe, I started doing this and got more clients. VO: He says each situation is unique. MALAYISHA: 05:39 Sometimes we walk through the border or at times we are on a truck. We fetch people from the Zimbabwean side at a petrol station and leave you on the South African side. VO: He negotiates with officials from either side and pays them a fee to turn a blind eye. To reach his final destination in Johannesburg, Thabane spent about R1000. R400 - for the Malayisha , who smuggled him to Musina. And R600 - to travel from the border town to Joburg. MALAYISHA: 04:44 We have an entrance gate where you pay R100 and the exit gate, you pay R100 and the bridge there are Zimbabwean soldiers, you pay R100. On the South African side, there are police, you pay R100. VO: Sometimes the business can be lucrative, he says. MALAYISHA:12:17 The biggest amount I have made is on many different occasions, the bigger the load the more I made. You can have 10 border jumpers and make R6000, the more the border jumper the more you can negotiate. He acknowledges that he is breaking the law but says the need to put food on the table far outweighs his conscience. MALAYISHA: 00:15 We are helping people at the same time, we get money. It is better than trying to find a job and I prefer to be self-employed I think i make more money. VO: He also prides himself on having escaped the consequences thus far. MALAYISHA: 07:39 I have never been into a police cell since I started doing my cross-border business, I always make sure I create good relations LINK 3 - But this is also about corrupt officials - not only on the Zimbabwean side but on the South African side too. This Malayisha says, some people bribe themselves out of providing COVID-19 certificates. MALAYISHA: 01:15 Here at the border, they are testing and ask for the certificate, but the issue is that if you do not have the certificate, they take money and let you go. Even if you have a certificate, they tell you it is fake and demand a bribe. ARRON MOTSOALEDI: 10:27 we have charged a number of home affairs officials who do the types of things you are saying. That is why we want to strengthen the anti-corruption unit, but more than anything else, you are aware that in the border management act, we want to have a commissioner of borders. VO: But it seems a better solution could be coming. The border management act was implemented last year. 11:24 The border management will coordinate that and will be able to identify syndicates because we know they exist. part of what they will do is devise play to catch these syndicates. VO: Thabani says his intention is not to break the law …all he wants is a chance at a better life. THABANI: 23:11I am hoping to go to SA safely and get work. Maybe the vaccines will help so things can go back to normal.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): From bribing officials to crossing the crocodile infested Limpopo River by foot, these Zimbabwean border jumpers are risking it all for a better life in SA.
metadata.Unique Selling Point: Images of panic and overcrowding at the Beitbridge border post are familiar enough to anyone who was watching the nightly television news over the festive season. But the reality and pain of such a life is unimaginable for most of us. In this report, we take a closer look at a day in the life of an illegal Zimbabwean border jumper. We take an emotional journey that uncovers who they are, the dangerous and illegal routes they use to cross into SA and how that is expected to affect our country's efforts of fighting COVID-19.
metadata.Summary: According to reports, thousands of desperate Zimbabwean nationals who were trying to cross into South Africa are no longer camping at the Beitbridge border post. But that doesn’t mean that they have returned to their Zimbabwean homes. Some have resorted to illegal and clandestine ways, like riding on canoes or bribing soldiers, to worm their way back into South Africa via the Limpopo River. This investigation explores how such longstanding issues of border security stand to hamper South Africa's fight against COVID-19.
metadata.Further information: In this report, we will speak to two case studies BEFORE their desperate attempt to cross via one of the 18 ports of entry of the Limpopo river. These people will share with us who they are, why they want to cross, their fears and hopes and aspirations for a better life in South Africa. In addition, we speak to one of the illegal operators of canoes, which are mostly used to carry people over to the SA side. These men accept money from travellers and their job is to transport them into SOuth Africa. How difficult is this job? Why aren't they getting caught? They will tell you that a big reason why they aren't in jail is because of the relationship that they have with the authorities, which, according to them, they share their profits with. We also attempt to answer questions around how such operations affect our COVID-19 infection numbers. Illegal crossers obviously don't require a negative COVID-19 test result to come into South Africa. How much of this is a threat to our health?
